title: adaptive-timeline-fragmenter-and-burst-convolution-reporter
author: Maya Patel
description:
Motivation: production traces show that short, high-intensity bursts (token surge windows) often dominate tail latency and cost but are poorly represented by existing sequence-mix samplers. This PR introduces two coordinated pieces: (1) Adaptive Timeline Fragmenter (ATF) — an instrumentation-aware runner that slices long sessions into context-coherent fragments while preserving KV-cache continuity for warmup analysis, and (2) Burst Convolution Reporter — a reporter that identifies burst windows and computes convolution-style burst metrics (burst-width distribution, intra-burst p50/p95/p99, inter-burst spacing histogram, and aggregate burst-shaped cost modeling).

What this PR does (summary):
- Adds a timeline fragmenter runner that can emit fragments with overlap and metadata tags to preserve warmup semantics for the serving runtime. Fragmenter supports several heuristics: energy-based (token entropy spike), fixed-time sliding window, and adaptive density thresholding.
- Implements burst detection and a burst-convolution aggregation pipeline that computes per-fragment and cohort-level burst metrics with optional symbolication hooks for prompt templates.
- Integrates new reporters into the existing bench harness and a lightweight visualization export (ndjson + small HTML viewer) for manual inspection.
- Adds end-to-end tests validating fragment warmup preservation and a synthetic workload generator that can inject controlled bursts for CI/benchmark regression tests.

Design notes / tradeoffs:
- The fragmenter emits fragments with an overlap window to preserve KV-cache warmup; overlap defaults to 64 tokens but is configurable per-profile. This trades some measurement duplication for more realistic latency during warmup-sensitive workflows.
- Burst convolution uses a sliding aggregation kernel; kernel width is configurable and documented. We intentionally avoid global normalization across sessions to keep cohort comparisons stable when input lengths vary.
- Memory overhead is small: fragment metadata is lightweight and the reporter streams aggregates to avoid holding full traces in memory.

Checklist:
- [x] Timeline fragmenter implementation
- [x] Burst detection and convolution reporter
- [x] Integration with bench harness config and example profiles
- [x] Unit + integration tests for fragment warmup semantics
- [x] Basic ndjson export and small visualization viewer (dev only)
- [x] Docs: bench/README and timeline-fragmenter.md

How to run locally:
1. Build the bench binary: make bench
2. Run the synthetic burst generator: ./bin/bench --profile profiles/synthetic_burst.json --mode generate --out /tmp/bursts.ndjson
3. Run fragmenter + reporter: ./bin/bench --runner fragmenter --profile profiles/timeline_fragmenter.json --input /tmp/bursts.ndjson --report out/burst_report.ndjson
4. Open dev viewer: scripts/viewer.sh out/burst_report.ndjson

Related: Linear ENG-3124 (profiling high-intensity bursts), BENCH-58 (bench reporting backlog). This PR is intended to be the baseline for follow-ups that will: (a) add automated regression thresholds for burst-shaped regressions, and (b) plug these metrics into the console alerting pipeline.

Notes on CI: initial run failed due to an ordering race in TestFragmentWarmup; added a coordination barrier and re-ran. All tests pass on linux amd64 and macos-latest.

Merge strategy: squash merge; keep commits focused and preserved in the squash message for auditability.
